title: "3. Finance and Risk"
aliases:
  - ../research/3-finance-and-risk.html
---

Clean power is cheap to build in most developing countries and expensive to finance, because investors price risks the project cannot control: a distribution company that may not pay, a plant that may not be finished, a currency that may fall and a state that may change the rules. Each risk has a different cheapest holder. This section of papers argues for removing payment risk at its source with a payment intermediary that guarantees the power contract rather than the debt, and then turning projects into a few standard securities: construction loans held by development banks, and pooled operating plants refinanced through first-loss equity and senior synthetic sovereign bonds. In stylized calibrations, the payment premium adds about 11 percent to a solar tariff, and refinancing pooled operating plants cuts the levelized cost of solar power by about a quarter. The host state's exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but it does not disappear.

## 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power {#paper-3-1}

*Removing offtaker risk at source in developing-country power markets*

Solar power is cheap to build in developing countries but dear to finance, because investors price the risk that a state-owned distribution company will pay late or not at all. A payment intermediary facility buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time, and collects arrears itself, behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance. Guaranteeing the contract removes the whole risk premium, about two dollars of saving per dollar of expected cost in a stylized case; guaranteeing project debt removes under a third of it. India's Solar Energy Corporation shows the design works, and its buyers' arrears show it needs utility reform.

## 3.2 From Projects to Asset Classes {#paper-3-2}

*Two-Stage Finance and Synthetic Sovereign Bonds for Clean Power*

Clean power plants in developing countries are financed one at a time, on bespoke terms, so each lender prices construction, payment, currency and sovereign risk together for the life of the loan. This brief proposes turning them into a few standard securities. Banks finance construction against a contingent purchase contract; once plants operate, their debt is refinanced into pools that issue first-loss equity, a thin mezzanine and a senior synthetic sovereign bond. Pooling across countries under one contract keeps the cushion thin, and refinancing cuts the price of solar power by about a fifth. Standardization, not subsidy, lowers the price.
